# Pasūra Sutta (Snp 4.8 (PTS Snp 161))
**ID:** Snp 4.8 (PTS Snp 161)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Pasūra Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp4.8
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Pasūra Sutta* is the eighth discourse of the *Aṭṭhakavagga* in the *Suttanipāta*, consisting of eleven stanzas numbered verses 824–834 in the standard Pali Text Society edition [Anderson & Smith 1913; Norman 1997–2001]. The text examines the futility and psychological hazards of ideological debate, emphasizing the drawbacks for both winners and losers alike [Hazra 1994; SuttaCentral]. Disputants seek praise and disparage opponents as fools, experiencing pride when victorious but distress and grief when defeated; in contrast, the detached sage who wanders without taking up dogmatic views offers no point of contention and achieves true purification [Hazra 1994; Lamotte 1970; Norman 1997–2001]. Modern scholars have discussed whether the sutta originally taught a philosophical quietism or "peace of noninvolvement" related to early ascetic skepticism, which was then integrated through its concluding verses (vv. 833–834) into the Buddhist path toward higher peace [Ruegg & Schmithausen 1990; Vetter 1988].
The sutta is addressed to an ascetic named Pasūra, who is directly named in verse 833 [Anderson & Smith 1913; Norman 1997–2001]. According to the *Suttanipāta* commentary, Pasūra was a wandering debater (*parivrājaka*) who famously carried a rose-apple (*jambu*) branch to challenge rivals; after suffering defeat by Sāriputta and ordaining under Lāḷudāyī, he subsequently attempted to debate the Buddha, on which occasion the Buddha delivered this discourse [Lamotte 1970]. An ancient canonical commentary is preserved in the *Cullaniddesa* or *Mahāniddesa* collection under the title *Pasūrasuttaniddesa* (Mnd 8) [SuttaCentral].
In early Buddhist parallel literature, a counterpart to the sutta is found in the Chinese translation of the *Arthavarga*, the *Yizu jing* (義足經, T 198), where the debater is named Yong ts'e (*Prasūra*) and sent by householders from Vaiśālī to debate the Buddha [Lamotte 1970; SuttaCentral]. Automated text-reuse data from DharmaNexus shows extensive verbatim shared material with the *Pasūrasuttaniddesa* (Mnd 8), alongside notable reuse in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Mahābyūhasuttaniddesa* (Mnd 13), and the *Mahāniddesa-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns segments of the sutta with passages in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26), the *Dīrgha Āgama* (T 1), and the Tibetan *Udānavarga* (D 326) [DharmaNexus].
